scenes.title: The Second Council of the Gods
scenes.summary: At dawn the gods sit in council, and Athena again tells of the sorrows of Odysseus, held by Calypso without ships or companions, and of the suitors' plan to kill his son on his way home. Zeus answers that the plan for Odysseus' vengeance was her own and bids her bring Telemachus home safely. He sends Hermes to tell Calypso that Odysseus is to go without escort of gods or men, on a raft, and on the twentieth day reach Scheria, where the Phaeacians will honor him like a god and send him home with more gifts than he would have brought from Troy.

scenes.title: Hermes at Calypso's Cave
scenes.summary: Hermes binds on his golden sandals, takes his wand, drops from Pieria to the sea and skims the waves like a gull to the far-off island. Around Calypso's cave grow alder, poplar and cypress where long-winged birds roost, a vine heavy with grapes, four springs and soft meadows of violets and parsley, and even a god stops to gaze. Calypso, singing at her loom, knows him at once and seats him on a throne; Odysseus is not there, but weeps on the shore as he always does. She asks why he has come and bids him come in.

scenes.title: Zeus' Command
scenes.summary: When he has eaten ambrosia and drunk nectar, Hermes tells his errand: he came unwillingly at Zeus' bidding, over endless salt water far from any city of men, to tell her to send away the most wretched of the men who fought at Troy. Calypso shudders and calls the gods jealous, who will not let a goddess take a mortal husband openly: so Artemis killed Orion, Dawn's lover, and Zeus struck Iasion with his thunderbolt for Demeter's sake. She saved Odysseus astride his keel and meant to make him immortal; since no god can evade the will of Zeus, let him go, though she has no ship to send him and can only counsel him. Hermes warns her to fear the wrath of Zeus, and goes.

scenes.title: Calypso Releases Odysseus
scenes.summary: Calypso finds Odysseus on the shore, his life ebbing away in longing for home: by night he sleeps beside her in the cave, unwilling beside the willing, by day he sits on the rocks and gazes over the barren sea. She tells him to stop mourning and build a broad raft, which she will stock with bread, water and wine and send off with a fair wind. Odysseus suspects some other plan and will not set foot on it unless she swears a great oath; Calypso smiles, calls him a rogue, and swears by Earth, Heaven and the water of Styx that she plans him no harm, for her heart is not of iron.

scenes.title: The Last Evening in the Cave
scenes.summary: Back in the cave they eat, he the food of mortals and she ambrosia and nectar. Calypso asks whether he still wishes to go: if he knew the sorrows ahead he would stay and be immortal, and she is no worse than his wife in form or stature. Odysseus answers that prudent Penelope is less than she in looks, being mortal, but he longs every day for home, and if some god wrecks him on the sea he will endure it. The sun sets, and they go into the inmost part of the cave and take their pleasure in love.

scenes.title: The Building of the Raft
scenes.summary: At dawn Calypso gives Odysseus a bronze double axe and an adze and shows him the tall, long-dead trees at the edge of the island. He fells twenty, hews and smooths them, bores and joins them with pegs and fastenings, and makes his raft as broad as the floor of a freight ship, with decking on close-set ribs, long side planks, a mast with its yard, a steering oar, and a fence of osier withes against the waves; Calypso brings cloth for the sails, and he rigs them and drags the craft down to the sea with levers. On the fourth day all is done.

scenes.title: Seventeen Days at Sea
scenes.summary: On the fifth day Calypso bathes and clothes him and sends him off with wine, water and provisions and a warm and gentle wind. He steers without sleeping, watching the Pleiades, late-setting Boötes and the Bear, which watches Orion and alone has no share in the baths of Oceanus, keeping it on his left as Calypso told him. For seventeen days he sails, and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains of the Phaeacians' land appear, like a shield on the misty sea.

scenes.title: Poseidon's Storm
scenes.summary: Poseidon, returning from the Ethiopians, sees him from the mountains of the Solymi and, angry that the gods have changed their plans while he was away, gathers the clouds, stirs the sea with his trident and looses every wind. Odysseus' knees give way: thrice blessed, he says, and four times, the Danaans who died at Troy, where he would have had funeral rites and fame; now he will die a wretched death. A great wave throws him from the raft and snaps the mast, and his clothes hold him under; he comes up spitting brine, struggles back onto the raft, and the winds toss it like thistles blown over the plain in late summer.

scenes.title: Ino's Veil
scenes.summary: Ino, daughter of Cadmus, once a mortal and now Leucothea of the sea, rises like a diving bird and tells him to strip, leave the raft and swim for the Phaeacians' land with her immortal veil under his chest, and to throw it back into the sea with his face turned away when he reaches land. Odysseus fears a trap and decides to stay on the raft while it holds; then Poseidon's wave scatters the beams like chaff. Odysseus bestrides a single beam, strips, binds on the veil and plunges in, and Poseidon, mocking him, drives his horses home to Aegae.

scenes.title: The Coast of Scheria
scenes.summary: Athena binds the other winds and rouses the North Wind to break the waves before him. For two nights and two days he drifts; on the third the wind drops, and from the crest of a wave he sees the land, as welcome as a father's recovery to his children. But the shore is cliffs and reefs with the surf roaring on them. A wave hurls him on the rocks, and at Athena's prompting he clings to one until the backwash tears him away, leaving the skin of his hands on the rock as pebbles cling to an octopus dragged from its den; he swims along outside the surf, looking for a beach.

scenes.title: The River God
scenes.summary: He comes to the mouth of a fair-flowing river, free of rocks and sheltered from the wind, and prays to its god as a suppliant; the river stays its current, makes a calm before him and brings him safely in. Swollen with sea water, breathless and speechless, he lies spent; when he revives he unbinds Ino's veil and lets it go into the river, and the current carries it back to her hands. He sinks down among the rushes and kisses the grain-giving earth.

scenes.title: Sleep under the Olives
scenes.summary: Fearing the frost and dew by the river and the wild beasts of the wood, he climbs to a thicket near the water, where a wild olive and an olive grow from one spot so thick that neither wind nor sun nor rain can pierce them, and heaps up a bed of fallen leaves. He lies down and covers himself, as a man on a lonely farm buries a brand in the ashes to keep the seed of fire, and Athena pours sleep on his eyes.

days.label: Day 7
days.note: The second council of the gods at dawn, Hermes' errand to Ogygia, Calypso's consent and oath, and the last evening in the cave (5.1–227). The poem tells Telemachus' days first and then returns to the gods; the count here takes the council as the morning after the last of them at Sparta (Day 6, 4.306–624). If it is the morning after the night that ends Book 4 in Ithaca (Day 4, 4.625–847), every day of this book is two days earlier.

days.label: Days 8–11
days.note: The building of the raft, from the first dawn after Hermes' visit (5.228) to “the fourth day, and all his work was done” (5.262).

days.label: Days 12–28
days.note: On the fifth day Calypso sends him from the island (5.263), and he sails for seventeen days, steering by the stars (5.263–278).

days.label: Day 29
days.note: On the eighteenth day the mountains of the Phaeacians' land appear (5.279–281); Poseidon raises the storm, the raft is wrecked, Ino gives Odysseus her veil, and Athena lays the winds (5.282–387).

days.label: Day 30
days.note: “There for two nights and two days on the swollen wave / he wandered” (5.388–389): the count here takes the day of the wreck as the first of the two days.

days.label: Day 31
days.note: On the third day the wind drops; Odysseus is thrown on the rocks, swims to the mouth of the river, and lies down to sleep under the olives (5.390–493).
